common_name: Early Sunrise Coreopsis (AAS-Winning Semi-Double Golden Tickseed)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost, or set out nursery transplants after frost danger passes, into well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Early Sunrise is a seed-grown selection bred to flower the first year and holds its compact, bushy form without staking.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Early Sunrise won the All-America Selections bedding plant award in 1989 for its ability to bloom heavily from seed in its first year, producing masses of semi-double, golden-yellow, two-inch daisy flowers with a slightly ruffled look on a tidy, well-branched plant that rarely needs staking. It is shorter-lived than the running threadleaf coreopsis cultivars, typically performing best as a strong bloomer for two to three years before needing division or replacement from fresh seed. In zone 9 heat, expect the heaviest flush in late spring with a lighter rebloom in fall if plants are sheared back hard after the first summer surge. Excellent drainage is essential in humid Gulf Coast summers, as crowns are prone to rot in heavy, wet clay.

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost, or set out nursery transplants after frost danger passes, into well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Sunray flowers reliably from seed the first year on a compact, well-branched plant.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Sunray earned the All-America Selections bedding plant award in 1990 for producing fully double, golden-yellow, pompon-like flowers on wiry stems from an otherwise typical single-flowered species, giving it a fluffier, more ruffled look than most tickseed cultivars. Bushy and free-branching, it flowers heavily from early summer into fall and holds up well as a cut flower thanks to its sturdy stems. Like other Coreopsis grandiflora selections it is relatively short-lived in the heat and humidity of the Gulf Coast, so allow some flowers to set seed for volunteer replacements or plan to start fresh seed every two to three years. Sharp drainage and lean soil keep plants compact; rich, moist conditions cause floppy, sparse-flowering growth.

common_name: Mesa Yellow Blanket Flower (AAS-Winning Compact Golden Gaillardia)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, or set out nursery transplants in spring, into very well-drained, lean soil in full sun; Mesa Yellow is an F1 hybrid bred to flower uniformly from seed in its first year without a cold treatment.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Mesa Yellow was the first Gaillardia to win an All-America Selections award, chosen in 2010 for its ability to flower quickly and uniformly from seed and for its heat and drought performance that held up through summer trial gardens across the country. Unlike bicolor blanket flowers, its ray petals are a solid, clear golden-yellow surrounding a slightly darker yellow-brown center dome, giving a cleaner, single-color look in the border. The compact, rounded habit stays well under a foot tall and needs no staking, and plants bloom continuously from late spring through fall with only light deadheading. Excellent drainage is critical in humid Gulf Coast summers, where standing water or heavy clay quickly leads to crown rot.

planting.note: Direct sow or set out transplants in spring into very well-drained, lean soil in full sun; in zone 9, Fanfare can also be started in late summer for fall establishment and bloom the following year.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Fanfare won an All-America Selections award in 2005 for its distinctive flower form, in which the base of each ray petal fuses into a narrow, trumpet-like tube before flaring open at the tip, giving the red-orange, yellow-tipped blooms a ruffled, almost fringed look that sets it apart from the flat-petaled species and standard hybrid cultivars. The unusual petal shape does not reduce pollinator appeal, and bees and butterflies visit it as readily as ordinary blanket flower. It flowers over a long season from late spring through fall on a compact, mounding plant that rarely needs staking. As with all Gaillardia, sharp drainage is the single most important factor for survival through humid Gulf Coast summers and wet winters.

common_name: Robert Poore Garden Phlox (Heat-Tolerant Mildew-Resistant Magenta Phlox)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, organically rich, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade, spacing generously for airflow; Robert Poore was selected in Texas specifically for resistance to powdery mildew in hot, humid summers.

directions: Plant in moist, organically rich, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade, with generous spacing for air circulation; Robert Poore is a heirloom Texas selection of garden phlox found growing in a San Antonio-area yard and prized for combining tall, vigorous, magenta-purple flower trusses with outstanding resistance to powdery mildew, the disease that disfigures most garden phlox by midsummer in the humid South. It has repeatedly ranked among the top performers for mildew resistance and heat tolerance in regional perennial trials, making it one of the most reliable tall garden phlox for Gulf Coast gardens. Plants form sturdy, upright clumps three to four feet tall that bloom from midsummer into early fall and draw butterflies and hummingbirds heavily. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in early spring, and remove faded flower heads before they set seed to prevent seedlings that revert to muddy magenta and gradually overwhelm the named cultivar.

common_name: Sherwood Purple Creeping Phlox (Deep Violet Woodland Groundcover Phlox)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in fall or early spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; Sherwood Purple spreads by surface stolons to knit together as a low, semi-evergreen mat.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; Sherwood Purple is a long-popular selection of creeping phlox valued for its saturated violet-purple flowers, a noticeably deeper and more vivid color than the species' typical lavender-blue, held just above a low, spreading mat of semi-evergreen foliage in mid-spring. Like the species, it spreads by surface stolons that root as they travel, gradually knitting together into a dense, weed-suppressing groundcover well suited to shaded slopes, woodland garden edges, and beneath deciduous trees. It performs best where summers stay relatively cool and humid soils are consistently moist, and like most Phlox stolonifera selections it struggles in the hottest, most humid zone 9 summers unless given a consistently cool, moist, deeply shaded microclimate with reliable irrigation. Shear lightly after flowering to keep the mat tidy and encourage dense regrowth; divide every few years if the center of the patch thins out.
